title: CSV and JSON files
plain: CSV and JSON are two text formats for data. CSV stores one row of values per line, separated by commas. JSON stores names and values in braces and brackets, and can nest lists inside objects.
check: A CSV row reads Alan,Manchester, UK and a program reads three values instead of two. Why does that happen, and how do you write the row so that it is read as two values?
rubric: Says the comma inside Manchester, UK splits the row into three values (Alan, Manchester and UK).
Writes the row as Alan,"Manchester, UK" with the value that contains a comma in double quotes.
Says to read CSV with a CSV reader (for example Python's csv module) and not by splitting each line on commas.
try: In a scratch folder create people.json that contains [{"name": "Ada", "city": "London"}] (use your editor). Run python3 -m json.tool people.json (python on Windows): it prints the same data neatly indented. Now change "name" to 'name' with single quotes and run it again: you get an error such as Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes, with a line and a column. Change it back and run it once more.
pitfall: Wrong belief: JSON is the same as JavaScript, so single quotes, comments and a last comma are fine, and every .csv file opens correctly in every program. Correct: JSON is strict, with double quotes, no comments and no comma after the last item. CSV has no single official standard, so commas, quotes and text encoding can differ between programs.

title: Files or database
plain: A file keeps data as text that you open and edit. A database keeps data in tables and answers questions about it. It also protects the data when several programs write at once.
check: Your todo app saves every task in tasks.json. Two browser tabs add a task at the same moment. What can go wrong, and what does a database do differently?
rubric: Says two writers can overwrite each other, because the whole file is rewritten and nothing coordinates them.
Says finding one task means reading the whole file, while a database can look it up by its id.
Says a file accepts any text, while a database checks the shape of the data.
try: In your project run git ls-files "*.json" "*.csv" "*.db" "*.sqlite". It lists the data files that Git tracks. Ignore settings files such as package.json. For each real data file, write down who writes it, who reads it and how many records it holds. A .db or .sqlite file in this list should not be in Git: see the SQLite card.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a database is only for big websites, and a JSON file is always simpler. Correct: a file is fine for small, single-user data that rarely changes. When data grows, is shared or must stay consistent, a database such as SQLite (which is itself one file) is safer.

title: Tables, rows and columns
plain: A table stores records in rows. Each column is one kind of fact, such as title. A primary key is a column whose value differs in every row, so one row can be found exactly.
check: In a todo table, two tasks are both called buy milk. How can the database tell them apart when you want to mark only one of them as done, and which column makes that possible?
rubric: Names the columns and a fitting type for each (id, title, done).
Chooses id as the primary key and says why title is a poor choice.
Inserts two rows with the same title and sees that this is allowed.
try: In a new scratch folder (mkdir sql-practice, then cd sql-practice) run python3 -m sqlite3 practice.db (Python 3.12 or newer; python on Windows; or sqlite3 practice.db if you have that program). Type CREATE TABLE todo (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, done INTEGER); then INSERT INTO todo (title, done) VALUES ('buy milk', 0); two times, then SELECT * FROM todo; You see two rows with the same title and the ids 1 and 2, printed like (1, 'buy milk', 0) (the sqlite3 program prints 1|buy milk|0). Now type INSERT INTO todo (id, title, done) VALUES (1, 'again', 0); and read the UNIQUE constraint failed error. Type .quit to leave. If python3 -m sqlite3 fails, run python3 --version: older Python versions lack this shell, so ask the tutor for another way.
pitfall: Wrong belief: any column can identify a row, and rows keep a fixed order. Correct: only a primary key identifies one row for sure, because titles and names repeat. A query returns rows in no promised order unless you ask for one with ORDER BY.

title: SQL basics
plain: SQL is the language of databases. SELECT reads rows, INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes rows and DELETE removes rows. WHERE chooses which rows; without it, UPDATE and DELETE touch every row.
check: Before you run DELETE FROM todo WHERE done = 1; how can you see exactly which rows it will remove, and what changes if you leave out the WHERE part?
rubric: Reads the WHERE clause and lists the exact rows that match.
States that a statement without WHERE changes every row.
Runs SELECT with the same WHERE first, to preview the rows.
try: In a scratch folder (for example mkdir sql-practice, then cd sql-practice) run python3 -m sqlite3 practice.db (Python 3.12 or newer; python on Windows; or sqlite3 practice.db). If practice.db already has a todo table, skip the CREATE TABLE line. Type these lines, each ending with a semicolon: CREATE TABLE todo (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, done INTEGER); then INSERT INTO todo (title, done) VALUES ('buy milk', 0); and INSERT INTO todo (title, done) VALUES ('call mum', 0); and SELECT * FROM todo; Then type UPDATE todo SET done = 1 WHERE id = 1; and SELECT * FROM todo; again: only the first row has done = 1. Now predict, then run UPDATE todo SET done = 1; with no WHERE: both rows change. Type .quit to leave, and keep practice.db for the next cards.
pitfall: Wrong belief: UPDATE and DELETE ask for confirmation, or I can undo them with Ctrl+Z. Correct: they run at once and the result is saved, and only a backup can bring the old data back. Without WHERE every row changes, so run SELECT with the same WHERE first.

title: SQLite
plain: SQLite is a small database that lives in one ordinary file, such as app.db. It needs no separate server, and Python includes it. It is a good first database for learning and for small apps.
check: Where does a SQLite database keep its data, and what happens to the data if you delete that file, or commit it to a public Git repository?
rubric: Creates practice.db with a table through python3 -m sqlite3 (or the sqlite3 program).
Lists the folder, finds practice.db, and says that all the data is inside this one file.
Adds *.db and *.sqlite to .gitignore, or says why a database with real data must not be committed.
try: In a scratch folder run python3 -m sqlite3 practice.db (Python 3.12 or newer; python on Windows; or sqlite3 practice.db). Type CREATE TABLE note (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, text TEXT); and INSERT INTO note (text) VALUES ('hello'); and .quit. Now run ls -l practice.db (PowerShell: ls practice.db): the file exists and its size is a few kilobytes. Open the shell again and type SELECT name FROM sqlite_master; to list the tables. The whole database is that one file.
pitfall: Wrong belief: SQLite is only for practice, and a real database always needs a server. Correct: SQLite is a real, widely used database engine that runs inside your program and keeps everything in one file. That is why the file needs a backup and must stay out of public Git.

title: Backup and restore
plain: A backup is a separate copy of your data, made at a known time. It only counts after you have restored it somewhere else and checked that the data is really there.
check: Your backup script runs every night and the file is there each morning. What have you not yet proven, and how would you prove it?
rubric: Says a file that exists each morning does not prove that the data can be restored.
Proves it with a restore test: opens the backup file on its own, somewhere else, and runs a SELECT that shows the expected rows.
Also checks how the backup is made (VACUUM INTO or .backup, not a plain copy while the app writes) and where it is stored (another disk or place, not a public repository).
try: In the scratch folder with practice.db (from the SQL basics card) run python3 -m sqlite3 practice.db, type VACUUM INTO 'backup.db'; and .quit. A second file backup.db appears (ls). Now run python3 -m sqlite3 backup.db, type SELECT * FROM todo; and .quit: your rows are there. That last step is the restore test. If backup.db already exists, VACUUM INTO stops with the error output file already exists: choose a new name such as backup-2.db.
pitfall: Wrong belief: copying the database file in a file explorer is always a good backup, and a backup file means I am safe. Correct: a copy made while the app is writing can be damaged, so use VACUUM INTO (or .backup in the sqlite3 program), or stop the app first. A backup is proven only by a restore test, and a copy on the same disk does not survive a disk failure.
